title: Inspect pyproject.toml before building a package
sources: Python Packaging User Guide: Writing your pyproject.toml; pip User Guide: requirements and constraints; Python 3.14 Standard Library: tomllib; reviewed 2026-10-03
masterChecklist: Dependency management, pip, requirement/constraint files, lock files, dependency vulnerability awareness
pyproject.toml, build backends, package metadata, wheels/sdists, versioning, publishing concepts
whyItMatters: Before a teammate can install a tool, its package metadata must say what it is, which Python it needs, and what build system will create it. An offline metadata check catches omissions before anyone installs or publishes anything.
simpleExplanation: pyproject.toml holds project metadata in [project] and build-tool requirements in [build-system]. A build backend takes the source tree and produces a wheel or source distribution; merely reading TOML does not build or publish either artifact. tomllib parses TOML into Python dictionaries, so a preflight script can check the fields. Runtime dependencies belong under project.dependencies, while build-system.requires lists packages needed to build. A requirements file tells pip what to install for an environment; a constraints file limits version selection but does not itself request installation. A lock captures a resolved environment, and dependency updates still need security and compatibility review.
mentalModel: The metadata is a shipping label. The build backend is the packing machine. A wheel is a prepared package and an sdist is source for a build. The preflight check reads the label; it does not start the machine or ship the parcel.
outcomes: Identify project and build-system metadata in TOML.
Use tomllib to validate a small package definition offline.
Distinguish requirements, constraints, and a resolved lock.

realWorldExample.scenario: A team plans to distribute a standard-library-only study report tool.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: A missing Python floor or build backend leads to confusing build behavior. An undeclared runtime package may work on the author's laptop but fail in a clean environment.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Inspect metadata, run tests in a clean environment, review any new dependency and its provenance, then build and inspect artifacts before any separate publishing decision.

workedExample.code:
import tomllib

metadata = b'''[project]
name = "study-report"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = []

[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=77"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"
'''
project = tomllib.loads(metadata.decode('utf-8'))
print(project['project']['name'])
print(project['project']['requires-python'])
print(project['build-system']['build-backend'])
print(project['project']['dependencies'])
explanation: The byte literal represents a local pyproject.toml sample; tomllib.loads accepts decoded text.
The [project] table describes the distributable tool and its supported Python baseline.
An empty runtime dependency list is deliberate because this sample needs only the standard library; it does not claim that setuptools is already installed.
The [build-system] table names an external backend that would be needed for a real build; this snippet only reads metadata and does not download or run it.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Remove the [build-system] table and observe which dictionary lookup fails. Restore it before considering a real build.

procedure: List the project's actual runtime imports and supported interpreter versions.
Write [project] metadata and a build-system table appropriate to the backend you deliberately choose.
Parse the file offline and check required keys before building.
Test a fresh environment so hidden global installs cannot mask missing dependencies.
Review dependency versions, licences, vulnerabilities and build artifacts; publishing is a separate authorized step.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a TOML parser run as proof that a wheel was built successfully.
commonMistakes.why: Parsing only checks readable data, not backend behavior or source layout.
commonMistakes.avoid: Perform a separate clean build and install test before release.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting a runtime library only in build-system.requires.
commonMistakes.why: Build dependencies and installed runtime dependencies answer different needs.
commonMistakes.avoid: Declare a true runtime requirement in project.dependencies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a constraints file installs its listed packages.
commonMistakes.why: Constraints restrict candidate versions when another command requests installation.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use a requirements/install request plus constraints when that workflow is appropriate.

lab.title: Preflight-check a fictional package definition
lab.safety: Parses an in-memory TOML sample only; no downloads, installs, builds or publishing.
lab.starterCode:

guidedSteps: Parse local TOML text with tomllib.loads.
Read the project name and dependency list.
Return those three facts without installing anything.
checks: Project name and backend are read correctly.
The empty runtime-dependency list counts as zero.
hints: The project and build-system sections are dict keys.
lab.solutionExplanation: Metadata inspection is a read-only browser exercise. It does not resolve, build or install packages.
challenges: Predict what happens if dependencies contains one package name.
Find the bug: reading the backend from the project table.
Experiment: remove requires-python and add a clear missing-field check.

projectConnection.milestone: Add an offline package-metadata preflight to CI before any build or release workflow.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: The preflight flags missing required fields, tests run in a clean environment, and no publishing happens as a side effect of inspection.

assessment.question: Does tomllib build a wheel?
assessment.answer: No. It parses TOML data; a separate build backend creates distributions.
assessment.explanation: Readable metadata is necessary but not enough to prove a build works.

assessment.question: Where does a library needed while the installed program runs belong?
assessment.answer: In project.dependencies, unless it is part of the standard library.

assessment.question: Does a constraints file by itself request installation?
assessment.answer: No. It constrains versions selected by an install request.
assessment.explanation: A separate requirement or install command names what to install.
